questions.topic: What A Type Hint Does Not Enforce
questions.learningObjective: state what a type annotation records and what it leaves to runtime
questions.stem: A function is written with an argument annotated as a list of integers and a return annotated as an integer, and a caller passes it a string. What does the annotation do about that call?

options.text: It records the intended types for a tool to read, and the interpreter never checks them at the call
It converts the string into a list of integers so that the annotation is true when the body runs
options.misconception: believes an annotation coerces the value into the type it names

options.text: It refuses the call, because the argument's type does not match the type the signature declares
options.misconception: believes the interpreter raises on a mismatched annotated argument

options.text: It records the intended types and the interpreter checks them only the first time the function is called
options.misconception: believes the check happens once and is then cached for later calls

questions.explanation: An annotation is a piece of metadata attached to a name at the moment the definition runs, and the interpreter stores it and does nothing else with it. There is no conversion and no refusal, so a caller may pass a string to a parameter annotated as a list of integers and the body receives the string. What the annotation is for is a separate tool, which reads the same metadata and reports the places where the code contradicts it, usually long before the program is run. That is why a function annotated as returning an integer can perfectly well return a string and print it, and why the annotation being present is never itself evidence that the code is right.
questions.hint: Ask whether the interpreter has to read an annotation to run the function at all.

questions.learningObjective: distinguish a structural protocol from a nominal abstract base class
questions.stem: Two ways exist to say a function needs an object with a name attribute. One names an abstract base class the argument must inherit from, and the other names a protocol. What separates the two?

options.misconception: believes the abstract base class matches on members and the protocol on inheritance

options.text: The protocol can only be used by the same package, while the base class is visible to any caller anywhere
options.misconception: believes a protocol is confined to the module that declares it

options.text: The base class provides a default implementation of every member, while the protocol requires each one written by hand
options.misconception: believes a protocol supplies working method bodies for its members

A protocol states the requirement by shape: the argument's class does not have to know the protocol exists at all, and what makes it acceptable is that it happens to carry the members. That difference is what lets code written against a protocol accept an object from a library whose author never heard of it, and it is also why a protocol is the better default for a function that only needs one or two operations from whatever it is given.

questions.learningObjective: explain what a bound on a type variable promises and what it still leaves open
questions.stem: A generic function declares its type variable with an upper bound, and a caller is offered three arguments to choose from. Which of the three does the bound actually permit?

Only that exact class and no other, because a bound names one concrete class rather than a family
options.misconception: believes a bound admits only the single class it names

options.misconception: believes a type bound is checked by nobody and restricts nothing

options.text: Only classes that inherit directly from the bound, excluding the bound class itself from the choice
options.misconception: believes the bound class itself is excluded by its own bound

questions.learningObjective: explain why a cast suppresses a report and what the writer becomes responsible for

A conversion of the value into that type, performed once when the cast is reached
options.misconception: believes a cast converts the value at the moment it is written

options.text: A deferral, since the checker will re-examine the claim once the whole file has been read
options.misconception: believes the checker returns to a cast later and confirms it

options.misconception: believes a static check is just a slower way of running the program

Rewriting the worst functions so the logic is genuinely clearer, because a low figure cannot be reached otherwise
options.misconception: believes a low complexity figure can only be reached by writing better code

@dataclass(order=True)
class Ver:
    major: int
    minor: int

print(sorted([Ver(1, 10), Ver(1, 2), Ver(0, 9)]))
print(Ver(1, 2) < Ver(1, 10))

questions.subject: PYTHON
questions.topic: What A Type Checker And A Runtime Test Each Buy
questions.learningObjective: explain the separate guarantees a static check and a test give, and where each fails
questions.stem: A team is arguing about whether adding a type checker or a test suite is the better use of a week. Explain what each one actually guarantees, and where each one is blind.

answer.exemplar:
The two tools answer different questions, and the argument dissolves once that is said out loud. A type checker reads code and reports where the code contradicts the annotations. Its guarantee is about code that has never run: an error path nobody has triggered, a call made with the wrong shape, a name that does not exist. That is a guarantee no test can give, because a test can only observe what happened. The checker's blindness is equally specific. It reads annotations, so it can only reason about types, and a right-typed wrong number sails straight through. It reads one file at a time and follows imports, so a wrong assumption about what a library does is invisible, since the library's own annotation says nothing about the condition it actually maintains. And it says nothing at all about a value, only about a type, so a division that cannot divide because the values are zero is not its business.
A test runs the program and compares what happened with what was meant to happen. Its guarantee is about behaviour, on the paths it actually drives, which is why it catches the wrong number that the checker cleared and the library that does not do what its signature implies. Its blindness is coverage: a branch nobody takes proves nothing, and the tests written last year describe last year's understanding, so a green suite is evidence about the paths it walks and silent about everything else. There is a third failure mode specific to types, which is worth naming because it is the one teams meet first. A checker is happy as soon as the annotations are satisfied, and an annotation can be satisfied by a claim, so a cast inserted to quiet a report converts a finding into an assertion nobody is checking. A cast with a comment saying why it is true is a legitimate boundary marker. A cast with no comment is a promise the codebase has stopped keeping.
So the week is better spent on both, and the ordering matters less than the discipline. Annotations first, because they are cheap and they make the next person's review shorter. Tests for the values, because values are where types stop helping. And a rule about what a test is allowed to let through: a test that asserts the type of a thing is usually a test that should not exist, because it will pass on a value that is right-typed and wrong.

questions.explanation: A type checker reads code without running it, so it finds wrong types on paths that have never been taken, and it is blind to values, to a wrong assumption about a library's behaviour, and to any annotation satisfied by a bare claim. A test observes only what actually happened, so it finds a right-typed wrong number and a dependency that does not do what its signature implies, and it is blind to everything the suite does not drive. The two are not substitutes, and a cast is the place the two meet badly, because a cast converts a report into a promise nobody is checking.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two needs the code to have run, and what a cast does to a report.

questions.subject: PYTHON
questions.topic: What A Virtual Environment Isolates
questions.learningObjective: explain what a virtual environment separates and what it does not
questions.stem: Two projects on one machine want different versions of the same library. Explain what creating and activating a virtual environment for each of them changes, and what it does not.

answer.exemplar:
The problem being solved is that the interpreter has one set of installed packages and one set of search paths, and two projects that want different versions of the same library cannot both be served by it. Creating a virtual environment gives a project its own directory containing its own interpreter link and its own site-packages directory, and activating it means the search path is arranged so that this project's directory is consulted and the machine-wide one is not. The two projects then each have a library version the other cannot see, and neither has to be installed twice into the same place.
What activation actually is worth saying plainly, because it is the part people get wrong. It is not a property of the environment, which is just a directory; it is a change to the shell's search path, made by running a small script that sets a few variables and, on some systems, points a command at the environment's interpreter instead of the machine's. That is why the change is undone by opening a new terminal, and why a script run from a different directory, or by an editor that does not go through the shell, sees the machine-wide packages rather than the project's. The environment is the isolation; activation is how one process is pointed at it.
Three things it does not do are worth naming. It does not isolate anything from the machine itself, since the interpreter, the compiler and the operating system libraries underneath are still the machine's, and a project needing a different interpreter version wants a separate environment tool rather than a virtual environment. It does not pin versions, because installing a library into an environment asks for a version at that moment and records nothing about the choice, which is why two people creating environments from the same requirements on different days can get different libraries; that is the job of a lock file. And it does not make the project portable, because the directory it created is full of absolute paths to the machine that made it and is not something to copy or commit.
The practical consequence is that a virtual environment is a per-machine, disposable thing that a project creates and throws away, while a lock file is a per-project, committed thing that travels. Keeping those two roles separate is what stops a team from either committing an environment or assuming a fresh one is reproducible.

questions.explanation: A virtual environment gives a project its own site-packages directory and its own interpreter link, so two projects can hold different versions of the same library without either seeing the other's. Activation is not a property of the environment but a change to the current shell's search path, which is why a new terminal or a tool that bypasses the shell sees the machine-wide packages instead. It pins nothing, since installing asks for a version and records no choice, and it is not portable because it is full of absolute paths, so a lock file is the committed half and the environment is the disposable per-machine half.
questions.hint: Ask whether the environment is a property of the project or of the machine, and what activation actually changes.

questions.subject: PYTHON
questions.topic: A Wheel Beside A Source Distribution
questions.learningObjective: explain what each built artefact contains and which one an installer should choose
questions.stem: A project publishes two files and a user installs the wrong one. Explain what each of the two contains, and which one an installer should prefer and why.

answer.exemplar:
Both files carry the same package name and version, and they differ in what has been done to the code and what the installer is expected to do next. A source distribution is an archive of the project's own files, laid out as they are in the repository: the modules, the tests, the configuration, the documentation, and whatever else the project chose to include. Nothing has been compiled and nothing has been recorded about the target machine, which is what makes it useful, because it is the one artefact that is guaranteed to exist for every version, including one where a build on the user's platform failed. It is also what an installer turns into the other kind, and what a person reads when they want to check what is in a release before running anything. What it costs is that something has to happen at install time: a build step runs on the user's machine, a compiler or a code generator may be needed, and the result can differ from one machine to another.
A wheel is the built output, already compiled, with the file names the interpreter expects and the metadata describing what it needs to be installed alongside. Nothing is built on the user's machine, so installation is a copy, it is fast, and it cannot fail for want of a toolchain. The trade is what goes into it: only the files that are meant to be installed, so the tests and the repository history are not there, and the choice of what to include was made when the wheel was built rather than when it is installed.
The rule that follows is short. An installer should prefer the wheel whenever one exists for the platform, because the user did not come to build the project. The source distribution is the fallback for a platform nobody published a wheel for, and it is also what a user needs when they intend to read, modify or rebuild rather than merely run. The two mistakes to name are the ones teams make in both directions: publishing a source distribution as the only artefact and making every user a builder, and installing from source on purpose in the hope of getting a different, better result, which is not what the source distribution does. The source is not a better wheel. It is a wheel with the build step left in.

questions.explanation: A source distribution is the project's own files unbuilt, guaranteed to exist for every version, and it makes the user a builder who needs a toolchain; a wheel is the built output with the file names the interpreter expects, so installation is a copy that cannot fail for want of a toolchain but contains only what was chosen for installation. An installer should take the wheel whenever a matching one exists, and keep the source distribution as the fallback for an unpublished platform and as the thing to read when the contents matter.
questions.hint: Ask what has been done to the code in each artefact, and who is made to build.

questions.subject: PYTHON
questions.topic: What A Build Configuration Has To Record
questions.learningObjective: explain the decisions a build configuration must record for a distribution to be installable
questions.stem: A project builds and installs on the author's machine and fails for a user. Explain what a build configuration has to record so that the second machine can install the result.

answer.exemplar:
A build configuration is the file that answers the questions an installer has to ask before it can do anything. The most important of them is the name and version, because a package cannot be installed, upgraded or depended upon without both, and the version is the only thing that tells an installer whether what it has already got is older than what it is being offered. Next is the list of requirements, with the range of versions that will be accepted rather than one exact version, and the convention is to state the floor and let the resolver find the ceiling, because a ceiling written into the project is a ceiling that stops being correct.
Then the list of things that are not code. A package that has a console command to offer has to say so, pairing the command name with the dotted path to the callable, and the same is true separately for the plug-in entry points a framework discovers. A package that ships data files has to declare them so that the built output contains them and the installer puts them where the code expects, and a package that reads files relative to its own source has to say that it is not safe to run from a compressed form. A package that needs a different interpreter version says so here, and this is the field that turns a confusing failure into a clear refusal.
Two things follow from this that are worth stating because they are where real projects go wrong. The configuration is not a script, and the fact that a tool reads it as data is what makes a build reproducible: the same configuration and the same inputs give the same output on any machine, whereas a step that reads the current date, the current directory or whatever happens to be installed locally is a step whose output nobody can predict. And a build has two sides, so the configuration has to cover what the tool does to the source and what the installer does to the result, and those are different audiences: one is a machine producing a file, the other is a program about to install it and needs to know what that file requires.

questions.explanation: A build configuration must record the name and version, the accepted version range for each requirement, the console commands and plug-in entry points offered, the data files to install alongside the code, and the interpreter version needed, because these are the questions an installer asks before it can act. It is read as data rather than executed, and that is what makes a build reproducible: a step that consults the date, the directory or whatever is installed locally produces output nobody can predict, and a configuration has to cover both the build's side and the installer's.
questions.hint: Ask what an installer must know before it can install anything, and what makes a build repeatable.

questions.subject: PYTHON
questions.topic: How A Resource File Is Reached At Runtime
questions.learningObjective: explain how code locates a data file that ships inside an installed package
questions.stem: A package ships a data file and code that needs it, and the code fails on a user's machine. Explain how a resource is meant to be located, and why the obvious approach breaks.

answer.exemplar:
The obvious approach is to work out the directory the current module lives in and join a file name onto it. That works on a developer's machine and fails on a user's, and the reason is worth understanding because it explains the whole design. On the machine where the project was written, the package sits in a source tree as a directory, and a path built from the module's own location finds the data file sitting beside it. Installed, the package may not be a directory at all: it may have been put inside a compressed archive and imported from there, and there is no directory to point at. Even when it is a directory, the code may have been moved to a cache elsewhere, so the location that worked when the package was written is not where the package is now. And in a frozen or single-file build the whole tree has been bundled into one artefact with its internal structure preserved in a table rather than on a filesystem.
The supported way is to ask the machinery where the package is, and to do it by package name rather than by a path the code assembles. The resource interface is given the name of the package and returns a traversable rooted at wherever that package is actually installed, and reading a file means joining a name onto that root and reading through the result. The root is a path-like object that presents the same interface whether it is backed by a directory or by an archive, so the code above it is identical in both cases, and the file name is separate from the location in a way that a hand-built path is not.
Two practical points go with this. A file that must be read and written, rather than merely read, cannot live among the resources, because an installed package's files are not the program's to modify, and the standard interface refuses the write. And the data files a distribution ships have to be declared in the build configuration, or the built output will not contain them and the read will fail on every machine including the author's, which is the symptom most often mistaken for a path problem.

questions.explanation: A path built from the module's own location works only while the package is an unpacked directory that still sits where it was written, and it fails when the package is imported from a compressed archive, has been relocated, or has been bundled into a single frozen file. The supported way is to ask the resource interface for the package by name and read through the traversable root it returns, which behaves the same whether it is a directory or an archive. A file that must be written cannot live there, and data files must be declared in the build configuration or the built output lacks them.
questions.hint: Ask what the package looks like when it is installed rather than when it is checked out.

questions.subject: PYTHON
questions.topic: A Long Function And A Flag Argument
questions.learningObjective: explain how to tell a function that is long for one reason from one that is long for several
questions.stem: A function has grown to eighty lines and takes a switch that selects between two behaviours. Explain how to work out what is wrong with it and what to do about each part.

answer.exemplar:
There are two separate problems in that description and they are often confused, so the first useful move is to tell them apart. Length is a symptom, not a diagnosis. A function is hard to read because it does several things, or because it does one thing through a great many cases, or because it is genuinely one thing that is simply long. The switch is the giveaway for the second case: a parameter that selects between behaviours means the function does more than one thing, and the eighty lines are the sum of both behaviours plus whatever they share. Reading it as one unit means reading two unrelated procedures that happen to share a name and a parameter list.
The refactor for the switch is to make the behaviours separate. Two named functions, each of which has to be understood on its own, is the honest shape, and it costs nothing in behaviour because a caller who wants one of them now says which one. Where the two genuinely share most of their body, the shared part is a helper and the two thin functions are what is left, and that shape also makes the next change easy, because a behaviour that has its own name can be changed without reading the other. The thing to be careful about is not over-splitting: a helper whose name is merely a restatement of its body, or one that takes six parameters to avoid a seventh, has moved the complexity rather than reduced it, and a reader now has to open two files to learn one thing.
For a function that is long because of one branch, the shape is different. A single branch that dominates the body, with everything else being a short common case, usually means one case has been growing by accretion inside a function that was written for the others. Extracting that case into its own function, with the common case left as the remainder, is a genuine improvement because each half then has one job and the call site says which case it is handling. What is not an improvement is splitting a straight-line sequence of unrelated statements into small functions just to reduce the line count, because the reader gains nothing and the names multiply.
The check on any of this is whether a reader trying to answer one question about the code has to read the whole thing. If the answer is no, the function is long for a reason you can name, and that reason is the thing to fix. If the answer is yes, it is too long, and the fix is to find what it is doing that the reader did not expect.

questions.explanation: Length is a symptom and a switch argument is a diagnosis: a parameter that selects between behaviours means the function does two things, so the honest refactor is two named functions, with the shared part extracted only where there really is a shared part. A function that is long because of one branch has usually had one case grow inside a function written for the others, and extracting that case leaves each half with one job. Splitting a straight-line sequence of unrelated statements to reduce the count just multiplies names, and the test is whether a reader answering one question still has to read the whole thing.
questions.hint: Ask whether the length is one thing done at length or several things done together.

def label(v: Union[int, str, None]) -> str:
    if v is None:
        return 'none'
    if isinstance(v, int):
        return f'int{v}'
    return f'str:{v}'

print(label(0) != label(None))

options.misconception: believes the checks are reached in the order they are written from the foot up
